title: Youth employment programmes improve labor-market outcomes on average, with effects shaped by design, context, and disadvantage
source_unit: International Labour Organization and World Bank, The Impact of Active Labour Market Programmes on Youth: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Impact Evaluations, 1990-2022
geography: Comparative systematic review of youth active labour-market programmes across 62 countries and low-, middle-, and high-income settings

denominator.unit: impact evaluations included in the systematic review

countries.unit: countries represented in the evidence base

interventions.unit: youth-focused interventions assessed within 171 active labour-market programmes

treatment_effects.unit: treatment-effect estimates synthesized across skills, entrepreneurship, employment services, wage subsidies, and public works

observations.method: ILO-World Bank systematic search and meta-analysis of counterfactual impact evaluations published between 1990 and 2022, using standardized mean differences and moderator analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The evidence base reflects available evaluations and may underrepresent low-capacity settings, null results, informal outcomes, or longer-run social effects; estimates are not a forecast for every programme.
observations.subgroup: Young people, programme participants, young women, disadvantaged youth, low-skilled youth, employers, training providers, and public employment services.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large evidence base does not make all programmes interchangeable; selection into programmes, implementation quality, local labor demand, and outcome definitions still shape results.

denominator.unit: youth active labour-market programme impact evaluations in the review

employment.value: well-designed youth active labour-market programmes have a measurable positive average impact on employment

earnings.value: well-designed programmes have a measurable positive average impact on earnings

income_group_pattern.value: average impacts are stronger in low- and middle-income countries than in high-income countries

observations.method: Meta-analysis of standardized treatment effects with comparisons by country income group, participant characteristics, programme type, and implementation context.
observations.uncertainty: Average effects do not establish that every participant gains, that gains persist, or that employment quality, bargaining power, or household security improve alongside employment or earnings.
observations.subgroup: Youth in low- and middle-income countries, young people facing labor-market exclusion, and participants entering work from unemployment or inactivity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher average impacts in lower-income settings may reflect larger unmet needs or lower baseline access, not a universal advantage of one programme model.

denominator.unit: youth ALMP design and subgroup comparison frame

stronger_types.value: entrepreneurship promotion and skills training report larger average impacts than employment services and subsidized employment programmes

priority_groups.value: effects are stronger for young women, disadvantaged youth, and participants under 25

design_features.value: soft-skills training, certification, combined interventions, and attention to multiple barriers are associated with stronger results

observations.method: Meta-regression and moderator analysis across intervention type, participant characteristics, country income group, design, and implementation features.
observations.uncertainty: Comparative effect sizes are not a simple ranking for policy adoption; programme costs, scale, implementation fidelity, selection, labor demand, and unmeasured outcomes can change practical value.
observations.subgroup: Young women, marginalized and low-skilled youth, participants under 25, youth with care or mobility barriers, and employers receiving trained workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skills or entrepreneurship programmes may perform well partly because they are targeted or paired with complementary supports; employment services or wage subsidies can be essential in other contexts.

denominator.unit: programme implementation and cost-effectiveness evidence frame

local_delivery.value: local and regional programmes often report better results than national programmes

partnerships.value: partnerships between public and non-public actors are on average more impactful in low- and middle-income countries

benefit_cost.value: three in four cost-effectiveness studies find benefits outweigh costs over the longer run

observations.method: Review-level comparison of programme scale, delivery partnerships, implementation features, and available cost-effectiveness studies.
observations.uncertainty: Cost-effectiveness evidence is available for a subset of programmes and varies in time horizon, costing conventions, outcome valuation, and transferability; local delivery can also vary in capacity and accountability.
observations.subgroup: Young participants, local governments, public employment services, training providers, employers, community organizations, and taxpayers funding programmes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local delivery can improve fit and reach but may fragment standards or create unequal access; national programmes can provide scale, portability, and more consistent rights.

related_sources.claim: ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026 provides complementary global youth, jobs-gap, informality, and job-quality context.
World Bank jobs research provides complementary labor-market policy and youth-employment context.

boundary: This record adds a youth-transition route linking active labor-market programmes to employment, earnings, skills, entrepreneurship, certification, gender, disadvantage, local delivery, partnerships, and cost-effectiveness. It summarizes evaluation evidence rather than respondent-level histories; it does not establish universal programme effects, job quality, household welfare, durable mobility, or causal effects outside the evaluated interventions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO publication page and report summary were reviewed for the 228-study, 62-country frame, intervention types, average effects, subgroup patterns, design features, partnerships, and cost-effectiveness claims.
